For the second method: when is an IQueryable actually executed, and what happens if callers add operations EF Core cannot translate? What should the method return instead?
exercises.expected_solution:
Problem 1 is lazy loading: it automatically loads related data as it is referenced, so each access to brand.Items inside the loop triggers an additional database query within the web request (~200 extra queries). Lazy loading should typically be disabled for web applications; its overhead goes unnoticed at development time when latency is small and test data sets are small, but in production — more users, more data, more latency — the additional requests cause poor performance. Fix with eager loading so EF Core executes a single query for the whole graph:

```csharp
var brandsWithItems = await _context.CatalogBrands
    .Include(b => b.Items)
    .ToListAsync();
```

(ThenInclude or string-based `.Include("Items.Products")` handle subrelationships; explicit loading is likewise not recommended for web apps because it adds extra round trips, and it's worth examining the actual queries for issues like Cartesian Explosion, which AsSplitQuery can address.) Problem 2: returning IQueryable means the statement isn't executed until enumerated; callers can further modify the query, but operations EF Core cannot translate produce errors that only occur at run time. It's generally safer to pass filters into the data access method and return an in-memory collection, e.g. `Task<List<SelectListItem>>` produced by awaiting `ToListAsync()`, which also executes the query immediately. Also use the async methods with async/await in web apps so web server threads aren't blocked during data access.
common_mistakes: Concluding 'the database is slow' and adding indexes/caching instead of recognizing the N+1 query pattern from lazy loading
Forgetting ToListAsync/ToList, so the 'query' is silently deferred and executes later than expected (or repeatedly)
Using explicit loading in the loop, which still makes a separate database round trip per entity
Using synchronous query methods in request handlers, blocking web server threads

exercises.title: Match the Workload to the NoSQL Store
exercises.problem_statement: Classify each workload as best served by a key-value store, document store, wide column store, or graph database, and justify each with the store's underlying abstraction and strengths: (a) an in-memory session/cache layer needing O(1) reads and writes of simple, rapidly changing data; (b) a product catalog whose entries have flexible, occasionally changing fields and must be queried by their internal structure; (c) petabyte-scale time-stamped sensor data requiring high availability and efficient retrieval of selective key ranges; (d) a social network's friend-of-a-friend recommendations with many many-to-many relationships.
hints: Recall each store's abstraction: hash table; key-value store with documents as values; nested map ColumnFamily<RowKey, Columns<ColKey, Value, Timestamp>>; graph of nodes and arcs.
Match the access pattern: O(1) simple operations vs querying inside a structured object vs huge ordered datasets vs traversing relationships.
For (c), which family of stores maintains keys in lexicographic order, allowing efficient retrieval of selective key ranges, and is used for very large data sets?
exercises.expected_solution: (a) Key-value store — abstraction: hash table. It generally allows O(1) reads and writes, is often backed by memory or SSD, and is used for simple data models or rapidly-changing data such as an in-memory cache layer; complexity shifts to the application layer if more operations are needed. (b) Document store — abstraction: key-value store with documents (XML, JSON, binary) stored as values. A document holds all information for an object, the store provides APIs or a query language based on the document's internal structure, documents may have fields that differ from each other, and document stores offer high flexibility for occasionally changing data (e.g., MongoDB/CouchDB offer SQL-like query languages). (c) Wide column store — abstraction: nested map ColumnFamily<RowKey, Columns<ColKey, Value, Timestamp>>; each value carries a timestamp for versioning and conflict resolution. Stores like Bigtable, HBase, and Cassandra maintain keys in lexicographic order for efficient retrieval of selective key ranges, and wide column stores offer high availability and high scalability for very large data sets. (d) Graph database — abstraction: graph, where each node is a record and each arc a relationship. Graph databases are optimized for complex relationships with many foreign keys or many-to-many relationships, such as a social network, though they are newer and tooling may be harder to find. Overall, NoSQL data is denormalized with joins done in application code, and most NoSQL stores favor eventual consistency (BASE: basically available, soft state, eventually consistent) over ACID.
common_mistakes: Picking a document store for the cache layer — it adds structure-querying machinery the workload doesn't need, when O(1) key-value access is the fit
Modeling many-to-many social relationships in a document store, which forces joins in application code instead of using a graph's native relationship traversal
Forgetting that most NoSQL stores lack true ACID transactions and favor eventual consistency, then assuming relational-style consistency guarantees
Treating the four store types as interchangeable 'NoSQL' rather than matching each abstraction to the access pattern

exercises.title: Add a Caching Layer Without Touching the Service
exercises.problem_statement: The homepage of your store runs three catalog queries (brands, types, paged items) on every request, and the data rarely changes. Design and sketch a caching solution that: (1) keeps caching logic out of the data access and UI code, (2) caches the paged items under a key that varies correctly per request, (3) uses a sensible duration, and (4) handles invalidation when an admin updates a brand. Use ASP.NET Core's IMemoryCache and explain your DI registrations.
hints: Separation of concerns: rather than editing CatalogService, what design pattern gives you an alternative implementation of ICatalogService that wraps the real one?
The items query takes pageIndex, itemsPage, brandID, and typeId — the cache key must include all of them. GetOrCreateAsync handles the fetch-or-populate logic.
For invalidation: a known key can be removed with _cache.Remove(cacheKey); when many entries depend on the same data, what token type lets you expire them all at once?
common_mistakes: Embedding caching calls inside CatalogService or the controller, violating separation of concerns and the Single Responsibility/Open-Closed principles
Using one cache key for all paged item requests, so users see another page's (or filter's) results
Choosing very long cache durations for marginal extra benefit while dramatically increasing stale-data risk
Never invalidating after updates, so admins can't see their own changes until expiration

topic_path: Testing Strategy and the Test Boundary

exercises.title: Triage the Test Suite
exercises.problem_statement: A team's suite has: 300 GUI-driven tests that exercise business rules through the UI and break whenever the layout changes; 40 tests that call a price-calculation method with various inputs entirely in memory; 12 tests that verify the repository layer reads/writes a real database; and 3 tests that drive the deployed system the way a user would. Classify each group (unit / integration / functional), explain which group violates the testing pyramid and the 'fragile test' principle and why, and say how the suite should be restructured.
hints: Definitions: a unit test runs completely in memory and in process, never touching file system, network, or database; integration tests verify code works with dependencies and infrastructure; functional tests verify the system from the user's perspective against its requirements.

The pyramid: a large base of unit tests, a smaller layer of integration tests, an even smaller layer of functional tests — each layer containing only tests that cannot be done adequately at a lower layer.
Fragile tests come from depending on volatile things (like the GUI) to test stable things (like business rules). Which group does that, and what kind of test should cover those rules instead?
exercises.expected_solution: Classification: the 40 in-memory price-calculation tests are unit tests (they test a single part of the logic, run completely in memory and in process, no infrastructure); the 12 repository-vs-real-database tests are integration tests (they verify code works with dependencies and infrastructure, with more complex setup/teardown such as restoring the database to a known state); the 3 user-perspective tests of the deployed system are functional tests (written from the user's perspective to verify the system meets its requirements). The 300 GUI-driven business-rule tests are the violation: they use a volatile thing (the GUI) to test stable things (business rules), the textbook fragile-test problem — unrelated GUI changes break many use case tests. They also invert the pyramid, which calls for a large base of unit tests, a smaller layer of integration tests, and an even smaller layer of functional tests, with each layer containing only tests that cannot be performed adequately at a lower layer. Restructure: design the system and tests so business rules can be tested without the GUI — e.g., a testing API with 'superpowers' (bypassing security constraints and expensive resources like databases, forcing the system into testable states) — converting the bulk of the 300 into fast unit tests of the business rules; keep only as many functional tests as needed to be confident the system behaves as users expect. Focus new unit tests on conditional logic, with at least one happy-path and one sad-path test for error conditions, rather than chasing code coverage metrics. Also avoid structurally coupling the test suite one-to-one to production classes, which makes production code hard to change and blocks the natural divergence where tests grow more concrete while production code grows more abstract.
common_mistakes: Calling the repository-database tests unit tests — anything touching a database is an integration test by definition
Fixing the fragile suite by adding retries or more GUI tests instead of moving business-rule verification below the GUI
Mandating one test class per production class and tests for every public method — structural coupling that makes production code hard to change
Maximizing code coverage (e.g., testing auto-properties) instead of focusing on conditional logic and things that can actually fail

exercises.title: Design the URI Scheme for a Bookstore API
exercises.problem_statement: Design the resource URI scheme for an online bookstore API that must support: listing all customers; fetching one customer; listing a customer's orders; creating an order; fetching one order; and listing the products in an order. Follow RESTful naming conventions (nouns, plurality, hierarchy) and explain how you handle the order-to-products relationship without making URIs too deep. Also show the request a client sends to create an order and what determines the new order's URI.
hints: Base resource URIs on nouns (the resource), not verbs (the operations) — the HTTP methods already imply the verbal action.
Collections are separate resources from their items: plural noun for the collection, then /{id} for an item; organize collection and item URIs into a hierarchy.
For the relationship chain customer → orders → products, recall the guideline limiting URI complexity to collection/item/collection, and break deeper navigation into separate lookups.
exercises.expected_solution: URI scheme: `/customers` (list all customers), `/customers/5` (one customer), `/customers/5/orders` (orders for customer 5), `/orders` (collection that order creation targets), `/orders/99` (one order), `/orders/99/products` (products in order 99). Use plural nouns for collections and organize collections and items into a hierarchy (`/customers` then `/customers/5`), and never put verbs in URIs — `/create-order` is the anti-pattern; the HTTP methods imply the action. For the relationship: avoid URIs more complex than collection/item/collection, so do NOT expose `/customers/1/orders/99/products`. Instead keep relationships simple and flexible: use `/customers/1/orders` to find a customer's orders, then `/orders/99/products` for the products in a given order — once an application has a reference to a resource, it uses that reference to find related items (and a better approach for discoverability is to include links in the response body, per HATEOAS). Creating an order: the client sends the order information in an HTTP POST request to the collection URI `/orders` (e.g., `https://api.contoso.com/orders`); the HTTP response indicates whether creation succeeded. The server — not the client — assigns the URI for the new resource. Additional cautions: avoid a large number of small resources (chatty APIs forcing many requests; consider denormalizing into bigger resources, balanced against fetching unneeded data) and avoid mirroring the internal database structure — the web API is an abstraction of the database, with a mapping layer if necessary.
common_mistakes: Putting verbs in URIs, e.g. /create-order or /getCustomer, duplicating what the HTTP method already expresses
Building deep nested chains like /customers/1/orders/99/products that are hard to maintain and inflexible if relationships change
Mixing singular and plural or using singular collection names (/customer, /order) instead of plural nouns for collections
Exposing one resource collection per database table, which increases attack surface and couples clients to the schema

exercises.title: Review a Flawed API Surface
exercises.problem_statement:
You inherit this API design:

```
GET  /api/getCustomerById?id=42
POST /api/customer/42/update-address
GET  /api/customers/42/orders/99/products/7/reviews
GET  /api/tbl_customer_addresses
GET  /api/orders/99/product-name
GET  /api/orders/99/product-price
GET  /api/orders/99/product-quantity
```

Identify every design flaw, naming the principle each one violates, and propose the corrected URI(s) for each.
hints: Scan for verbs in paths, query-parameter lookups that should be hierarchy, nesting depth, anything leaking the database, and endpoints so small that clients must make many calls.
The guideline caps URI complexity at collection/item/collection; what should replace the five-segment chain?
Three endpoints each return one field of the same order — what does the guidance about 'chatty web APIs' and 'a large number of small resources' say to do instead?
exercises.expected_solution: Flaws and fixes: (1) `GET /api/getCustomerById?id=42` puts a verb in the URI and bypasses the resource hierarchy — use nouns, not verbs, since GET already implies retrieval: `GET /customers/42`. (2) `POST /api/customer/42/update-address` uses a verb plus a singular collection noun — collections should be plural nouns, and the operation belongs to the method, not the path: update the customer resource at `/customers/42` (address being part of its representation). (3) `/customers/42/orders/99/products/7/reviews` allows navigation through several levels of relationships — URIs should not be more complex than collection/item/collection because deep chains are difficult to maintain and inflexible if relationships change; replace with simpler steps such as `/customers/42/orders` to list orders, then `/orders/99/products`, then `/products/7/reviews`. (4) `/api/tbl_customer_addresses` mirrors the internal database structure — the web API shouldn't expose each table as a collection of resources (it increases attack surface and risks data leakage); model business entities instead and introduce a mapping layer between database and API, e.g. addresses as part of `/customers/{id}`. (5) The three one-field endpoints (`product-name`, `product-price`, `product-quantity`) create a chatty web API with a large number of small resources, forcing clients to send multiple requests to gather data; every web request imposes load on the server. Combine related information into a bigger resource retrievable in a single request: `GET /orders/99` (or `/orders/99/products`) returning a representation containing name, price, and quantity — balanced against the overhead of returning data clients don't need.
common_mistakes: Fixing the verb URIs by just renaming them (e.g., /fetchCustomer) instead of removing operations from paths entirely
Over-correcting chattiness by returning enormous denormalized objects, ignoring the latency and bandwidth cost of fetching data the client doesn't need
Leaving the database table exposure in place but renaming it cosmetically, rather than introducing an abstraction/mapping layer over business entities
Keeping deep nesting because 'it documents the relationship' — links in the response body (HATEOAS) are the recommended way to expose associations

exercises.title: Choose the Method and Status Code
exercises.problem_statement: For an e-commerce API with `/customers` and `/customers/{id}`, specify the correct HTTP method, the success status code(s), and key error codes for each operation — then answer the two follow-ups. Operations: (a) create a new customer; (b) fully replace customer 1's details; (c) change only customer 1's price-tier field, deleting their legacy 'color' preference field, using a JSON-based patch format (name the media type and show the patch document for an original resource `{"name":"gizmo","category":"widgets","color":"blue","price":10}` that sets price to 12, removes color, and adds size 'small'); (d) delete customer 1. Follow-ups: (e) what should the server return if a client POSTs to `/customers/1` to choose its own URI? (f) what does the server return when the request's Content-Type media type is unsupported, and when nothing in the Accept header can be matched?
hints: POST targets the collection URI and the server assigns the new resource's URI; PUT targets an individual item with a complete representation and must be idempotent.
For (c): JSON merge patch documents mirror the resource's structure, include only the fields to change or add, and use null to delete a field; its media type embeds 'merge-patch'.

Status code table highlights: created resources → 201 with Location header; successful delete → 204; malformed patch → 400 vs patch valid but inapplicable → 409; media type problems → 415 (request body format) vs 406 (response format).
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Create: POST to `/customers` (the collection). Success: 201 (Created) with the new resource's URI in the Location header and a representation in the body; 400 (Bad Request) for invalid data. (b) Full replace: PUT to `/customers/1` with a complete representation of the resource. Success: 200 (OK), or 204 (No Content) when no body is returned; 201 (Created) if the route supports creation via PUT and the resource didn't exist; 409 (Conflict) if the request conflicts with the resource's current state. PUT must be idempotent — resubmitting the same request leaves the same resource with the same values. (c) Partial update: PATCH to `/customers/1` using JSON merge patch, media type `application/merge-patch+json`. The patch document has the same structure as the original resource but includes only fields to change or add, with null deleting a field:

```json
{
    "price": 12,
    "color": null,
    "size": "small"
}
```

This updates price, deletes color, adds size, and leaves name and category unmodified. (Caveat: merge patch is unsuitable if the resource can hold explicit null values and doesn't specify the order updates apply; JSON patch, `application/json-patch+json`, is more flexible — a sequence of add/remove/replace/copy/test operations.) PATCH statuses: 200 (OK) on success; 400 (Bad Request) for a malformed patch document; 409 (Conflict) when the patch is valid but can't be applied to the resource in its current state; 415 (Unsupported Media Type) when the patch format isn't supported. (d) Delete: DELETE to `/customers/1`. Success: 204 (No Content); 404 (Not Found) if the resource doesn't exist. (e) The client shouldn't attempt to create its own URI; it should POST to the collection and let the server assign the URI. A POST to a specific URI like `/customers/1` should get 400 (Bad Request) — per the conventions table, POST to an individual item URI is an error (405 Method Not Allowed applies when a URI doesn't support POST at all). (f) Unsupported request media type → 415 (Unsupported Media Type); when the server can't match any media type listed in the Accept header → 406 (Not Acceptable).
common_mistakes: Using PUT with a partial body to do a partial update — PUT requires a complete representation; PATCH exists for partial changes
Returning 200 without a Location header on resource creation instead of 201 (Created) plus the new URI in Location
Confusing 415 (server can't process the request's media type) with 406 (server can't produce any media type the Accept header allows)
Treating POST or PATCH as idempotent like PUT — they aren't guaranteed to be, so blind retries can duplicate effects

exercises.title: Version the Customer API Without Breaking Anyone
exercises.problem_statement: Your public customer API must restructure the flat `address` string into subfields (streetAddress, city, state, zipCode) — a breaking change for existing partner clients you don't control. Many clients sit behind older caching proxies, and your API makes heavy use of HATEOAS links. Compare the four explicit versioning mechanisms (URI, query string, header, media type) on: how the client requests version 2, the impact on caching, and the impact on HATEOAS. Recommend one mechanism for this scenario and justify it. Also: why is adding a 'dateCreated' field NOT a breaking change in the first place?
hints: Write a sample v2 request for each mechanism: a version segment in the path, ?version=2, a custom header like Custom-Header: api-version=2, and Accept: application/vnd.contoso.v1+json.

Cache-friendliness depends on whether the version is visible in the URI/query string or hidden in headers — and note the warning about older browsers and proxies not caching URIs that include query strings.
For HATEOAS, ask which mechanism lets links carry version information naturally via MIME types rather than rewriting every URI or requiring custom headers.
exercises.expected_solution: URI versioning: client calls `https://api.contoso.com/v2/customers/3`; simple, but the server must route to the right endpoint and it becomes unwieldy as many versions accumulate; purists object that the same data (customer 3) shouldn't have different URIs per version; it complicates HATEOAS because all links must include the version number; cache-friendly since the same URI always refers to the same data. Query string versioning: `https://api.contoso.com/customers/3?version=2` (default to a meaningful value like 1 when omitted); semantic advantage that the same resource is always retrieved from the same URI, but request-handling code must parse the query string; complicates HATEOAS the same way; nominally cache-friendly, but some older web browsers and web proxies don't cache responses for requests that include a query string, which can degrade performance. Header versioning: custom header such as `Custom-Header: api-version=2`; requires clients to add the header on every request (default when omitted); links must include the appropriate custom header for HATEOAS; requires more logic to examine header values and, in large-scale environments, many client versions can cause significant duplicated data in server-side caches — and caching proxies that key only on URI are a problem. Media type versioning: `Accept: application/vnd.contoso.v1+json`, with the server confirming via Content-Type, returning 406 (or a default) if no known media type is given; straightforward and well-suited for HATEOAS since links can include the MIME type of related data; like header versioning, it needs more logic to inspect the Accept header and can duplicate cached data. Recommendation for this scenario: with older caching proxies in play (which may serve stale or wrong-version responses for header-varied requests, and may not cache query strings) and heavy HATEOAS use, the trade-off is between URI versioning (best for the old proxies, worst for HATEOAS link maintenance) and media type versioning (best for HATEOAS, weaker for proxy caching). Given the explicit caching constraint, URI versioning is the defensible pick: `/v2/...` URIs are unambiguous to every cache, existing v1 URIs continue to operate normally returning the original schema, and the HATEOAS cost is mechanical (links carry the version in their URIs). The dateCreated follow-up: adding content to existing resources might not be breaking because clients that aren't expecting the field simply ignore unrecognized fields and continue functioning; breaking changes are drastic schema modifications like field removals or renames, or changed relationships — such as the address restructuring.
common_mistakes: Treating any schema change as breaking — additive fields that clients can ignore usually aren't; removals, renames, and restructures are
Choosing header or media type versioning without accounting for caches/proxies that key only on the URI, causing duplicated cache data or wrong-version responses
Forgetting a default version when the query parameter or header is omitted, instantly breaking all existing clients
Ignoring HATEOAS: whatever mechanism is chosen, every link must consistently carry the version (URI segment, query string, header, or MIME type)

exercises.title: Audit the Order Service's Request Handling
exercises.problem_statement: Review three behaviors in an order-management API: (1) DELETE /orders/7 returns 204 the first time and 404 when repeated — a teammate files a bug saying 'DELETE isn't idempotent'. (2) POST /orders creates the order but also resets every customer's marketing preferences as a side effect. (3) A mobile client renders an order screen by calling GET /orders/{id}/status, then GET /orders/{id}/items, then GET /orders/{id}/shipping, then GET /orders/{id}/billing — four round trips per screen. Judge each behavior against web API implementation best practices: which are defects, which are fine, and what is the fix for each defect?
hints: Idempotency is about resource state, not response codes: does repeating the same request leave the system in the same state? The spec for this scenario explicitly discusses differing status codes.
POST effects should be scoped: limited to the new resource and possibly directly related resources — measure behavior (2) against that rule.
Behavior (3) is the 'chatty' anti-pattern: every request carries protocol, network, and compute overhead. What coarser-grained design (and what verb support on collections) reduces round trips?
exercises.expected_solution: (1) Not a defect. Idempotency means the same request repeated over the same resource results in the same state — the code implementing the request should impose no side-effects on repetition. Sending multiple DELETE requests to the same URI has the same effect on state, although the HTTP status code may differ: the first DELETE returns 204 (No Content) and subsequent ones 404 (Not Found). The differing status codes don't violate idempotency. (2) Defect. If a POST creates a new resource, the effects should be limited to the new resource and possibly directly related resources — e.g., an e-commerce POST creating an order might also amend inventory levels and generate billing information — but it should not modify information not directly related to the order or have other side-effects on the overall state of the system. Resetting all customers' marketing preferences is an unrelated global side effect; remove it from the POST handler. (3) Defect: a chatty API. Every request comes with protocol, network, and compute overhead — 100 small requests instead of one batch incur added overhead at the client, on the network, and at the resource server. Fix by avoiding chatty operations: return a coarser-grained order representation so one GET supplies what the screen needs, and more generally provide HTTP verb support for resource collections, not just individual resources (a GET on a collection retrieves multiple resources at once; POST can add multiple new resources to a collection; PUT can replace a collection's entire set; DELETE can remove an entire collection); request batching (e.g., the OData batch support in ASP.NET Web API 2) lets a client package several requests into a single HTTP request/response.
common_mistakes: Equating idempotency with identical status codes on every repeat, rather than identical resulting resource state
Defending unrelated POST side effects as 'business logic' — directly related effects (inventory, billing for the order) are fine; global unrelated mutations are not
Fixing chattiness client-side with parallel requests instead of redesigning the API to expose coarser-grained resources or batch/collection operations
Swinging to the opposite extreme and returning enormous payloads full of data the client never uses

exercises.title: Stop the Lost Updates with ETags
exercises.problem_statement: Two back-office users load order 1 at the same time, edit different fields, and save one after the other — the second save silently erases the first user's change. Design the optimistic-concurrency flow that prevents this lost update, using ETags: specify (1) what the server includes when the order is first fetched, (2) what header the client sends on its PUT and with what value, (3) the three server-side comparison outcomes and the exact status code for each, and (4) what each status tells the client to do with its cached copy. Include a sample PUT request.
hints: On GET, the response carries an opaque string that changes every time the resource changes — the client must cache it alongside the data.
On update, the relevant header is If-Match (If-None-Match is the read-side optimization for 304s).
Three outcomes: ETags match → perform the update; ETags differ → someone else changed it; resource gone → not found. Map each to 204 / 412 / 404.
exercises.expected_solution:
(1) When the client GETs the order, the response includes an ETag header — an opaque string indicating the version of the resource; each time the resource changes, the ETag changes. The client caches the ETag as part of the data (e.g., ETag: "2282343857"). (2) On update, the client sends a PUT containing the new details plus an If-Match header referencing the cached ETag:

```http
PUT https://adventure-works.com/orders/1 HTTP/1.1
If-Match: "2282343857"
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

productID=3&quantity=5&orderValue=250
```

(3) The server obtains the current ETag for the resource and compares it with the If-Match value: (a) ETags match → the resource hasn't changed; the server performs the update and returns 204 (No Content), optionally with Cache-Control and ETag headers for the updated version, and always a Location header referencing the updated resource's URI; (b) ETags don't match → the data was changed by another user since it was fetched; the server returns 412 (Precondition Failed) with an empty body and does not apply the update; (c) the resource no longer exists → 404 (Not Found). (4) Client cache handling: on 204 the object can remain cached (as long as Cache-Control isn't no-store) but the ETag must be updated; on 412 or 404 the cached object should be discarded — for 412 the client should re-fetch the current version (getting the new ETag) before retrying. Crucially, the If-Match header is optional, and if it's omitted the API will always attempt the update, possibly blindly overwriting another user's change — to avoid lost updates, always provide If-Match. This is exactly what fixes the two-user scenario: the second user's stale ETag fails the comparison and they get 412 instead of silently clobbering the first save.
common_mistakes: Sending If-None-Match on the PUT — that header optimizes GETs (returning 304 Not Modified); updates use If-Match
Omitting If-Match entirely, so the server blindly overwrites concurrent changes — the original lost-update bug
Returning 409 or 400 when the ETag comparison fails instead of 412 (Precondition Failed)
Keeping the stale cached object and old ETag after a 412, guaranteeing the next retry fails the same way

exercises.title: Design the Report Generator's Async API
exercises.problem_statement: POST /reports kicks off a financial-report generation that takes 5–10 minutes. Today the handler blocks until the report is done, so clients time out, and a load balancer added for scale breaks things because request N depends on state left in server memory by request N-1. Design the corrected flow: (1) the immediate response to the POST, (2) how the work is tracked and executed, (3) the polling endpoint and what it returns while running, when complete, and when failed, and (4) the statelessness rule that makes the API safe to scale horizontally — explain why it also improves availability.
hints: A long-running request should be validated, handed to a separate task, and answered immediately — with which status code, and carrying what URI back to the client?
Track the request in a table (e.g., Azure Table Storage or Redis) under a unique key such as a GUID, recording state transitions Running → Complete/Failed.
For scaling: what must be true of each request so that any instance behind the load balancer can serve it, and what does that buy you when a server dies?
exercises.expected_solution: (1) The web API performs some initial checking to validate the request, initiates a separate task to perform the work, and immediately returns 202 (Accepted) — indicating the request was accepted for processing but is incomplete — with a URI containing a unique key for polling, e.g. /polling/{guid}. (2) Tracking and execution: store information about the request in a table held in Azure Table Storage or Azure Managed Redis (or send it via Azure Service Bus), generating a unique key (such as a GUID) for the entry; initiate processing as a separate task or with a library like Hangfire, recording the task's state as Running; when the task completes, store the results and set state to Complete; on failure, store failure information and set state to Failed, applying retry techniques for possibly transient failures. (If the process has more intermediate states, use a library supporting the saga pattern, like NServiceBus or MassTransit.) (3) Polling: while the task runs, the client periodically sends requests to the polling URI; the endpoint queries the task's state in the table and returns 200 (OK) containing the state (Running, Complete, or Failed); once completed or failed, the response can also include the processing results or available failure information. Alternatives to polling include push notifications via a notification hub, the Comet model over a persistent connection, or SignalR. (4) Statelessness: each request must be atomic, with no dependencies between one client request and subsequent ones — that's what the in-memory-state design violated. This supports scalability because web service instances can be deployed across multiple servers, client requests can be directed at any instance, and the results are always the same. It also improves availability: if a web server fails, requests can be routed to another instance (e.g., via Azure Traffic Manager) while the server restarts, with no ill effects on clients.
common_mistakes: Returning 200 or 201 immediately even though processing hasn't completed — 202 (Accepted) is the code for accepted-but-incomplete work
Returning 202 with no polling URI or unique key, leaving the client no way to learn the outcome
Storing job state in a single server's memory, which breaks as soon as a load balancer routes the poll to a different instance
Reporting only success from the status endpoint, with no Failed state or failure information for the client

exercises.title: CP or AP: Classify Two Data Stores Under Partition
exercises.problem_statement: Your company runs two systems on a distributed data store. System 1 is a payment ledger: the business requires atomic reads and writes, and returning stale balances is unacceptable even if some requests must fail with an error. System 2 is a social activity feed: it must keep responding to every request even during network failures, and showing a slightly outdated feed is acceptable. A network partition splits the cluster in two. For each system, classify the appropriate design as CP or AP under the CAP theorem, explain why partition tolerance is not optional, and name the consistency model (strong, eventual, or weak) that best matches each system.
hints: Recall the three CAP guarantees: Consistency (every read receives the most recent write or an error), Availability (every request receives a response, possibly not the latest version), and Partition Tolerance (the system continues to operate despite network partitioning).
Networks aren't reliable, so partition tolerance must be supported. The real trade-off is therefore between consistency and availability when a partition occurs.

Ask for each system: when the partition happens, would the business rather wait or error (possibly timing out on the partitioned node), or return the most readily available version of the data on any node?
exercises.expected_solution:
Partition tolerance is mandatory in both cases because networks aren't reliable -- you cannot choose CA; the software trade-off is between consistency and availability during a partition.

System 1 (payment ledger) should be CP: the business needs atomic reads and writes, so during a partition the system waits for the partitioned node to respond, which may result in a timeout error. Returning an error is acceptable; returning a stale balance is not. This matches strong consistency: after a write, reads will see it, with data replicated synchronously (the model used by file systems and RDBMSes, suited to systems that need transactions).

System 2 (social feed) should be AP: responses return the most readily available version of the data on any node, which might not be the latest, and writes propagate when the partition resolves. This matches eventual consistency: after a write, reads will eventually see it (typically within milliseconds) because data is replicated asynchronously -- a good fit for highly available systems (the approach used by DNS and email).
common_mistakes: Treating CAP as a free choice of any two and proposing a 'CA' system, ignoring that network partitions will happen and partition tolerance must be supported
Confusing availability in the CAP sense (every request gets a response, possibly stale) with high uptime
Mapping the payment ledger to eventual consistency because it is 'fast enough', when the requirement of atomic reads and writes demands strong consistency
Assuming an AP system permanently loses the writes made during a partition, when in fact writes take some time to propagate after the partition is resolved

exercises.title: Compute Composite Availability for a Two-Tier Service
exercises.problem_statement: A service consists of an application tier (Foo) that calls a database (Bar); a request must pass through both, so they are in sequence. Each component has 99.9% availability on its own. (a) Compute the overall availability of the service and state roughly how much downtime per year 99.9% alone corresponds to. (b) The team duplicates the database into two redundant instances so that the database layer works if either instance is up (in parallel). Compute the availability of the database layer and the new end-to-end availability of Foo followed by the redundant Bar layer. (c) Explain why adding a component in sequence decreases overall availability while adding one in parallel increases it.
hints: For components in sequence the formula is Availability(Total) = Availability(Foo) * Availability(Bar); for components in parallel it is Availability(Total) = 1 - (1 - Availability(Foo)) * (1 - Availability(Bar)).
Work with decimals: 99.9% = 0.999, so the unavailability of one component is 0.001. In parallel, both copies must be down at the same time for the layer to be down.
(a) 0.999 * 0.999; (b) parallel layer: 1 - (0.001 * 0.001) = 0.999999, then multiply by 0.999 for the serial app tier; for downtime, three nines is on the order of 8h 45min per year.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) In sequence: 0.999 * 0.999 = 0.998001, i.e. about 99.8% availability -- worse than either component alone. A single component at 99.9% corresponds to roughly 8h 45min 57s of downtime per year (about 43m 50s per month, 10m 5s per week, 1m 26s per day). For comparison, 99.99% (four nines) allows only about 52min 35.7s per year.

(b) The redundant database layer in parallel: 1 - (1 - 0.999) * (1 - 0.999) = 1 - 0.000001 = 0.999999, i.e. 99.9999%. End-to-end: 0.999 * 0.999999 = 0.998999..., about 99.9% -- the serial app tier is now the dominant source of unavailability.

(c) In sequence, a request fails if either component is down, so unavailabilities compound and total availability decreases below the weakest component. In parallel, the layer fails only if all redundant copies are down simultaneously, so the unavailabilities multiply (0.001 * 0.001) and total availability increases. This is why availability is quantified in 'number of 9s' and why redundancy (fail-over and replication) is the standard way to add nines.
common_mistakes: Averaging the availabilities of serial components instead of multiplying them
Using the series formula for the parallel case (or vice versa), e.g. computing 0.999 * 0.999 for the redundant pair
Forgetting to multiply the parallel layer's availability by the remaining serial component, reporting 99.9999% as the end-to-end figure
Mixing up the downtime budgets for three nines (about 8h 45min/year) and four nines (about 52min/year)

exercises.title: Choose a Fail-Over Pattern for a Public API
exercises.problem_statement: A team must add high availability to a public-facing API currently served by one machine. Option A is active-passive fail-over: a standby server receives heartbeats from the active server and takes over the active server's IP address if the heartbeat is interrupted. Option B is active-active fail-over: both servers manage traffic, spreading load between them. The product owner asks: which option recovers faster, which one helps with load, what data-loss risk both options share, and what extra requirement active-active imposes on a public-facing deployment? Recommend an option for an API whose traffic is growing quickly and justify it.
hints: In active-passive, the length of downtime is determined by whether the passive server is already running in 'hot' standby or must boot from 'cold' standby; only the active server handles traffic.
In active-active, both servers manage traffic. Think about what the outside world (DNS) or internal callers need to know for traffic to reach both servers.
The shared risk: what happens to newly written data if the active system fails before that data has been replicated to the other server?
exercises.expected_solution:
Recovery speed: active-passive downtime depends on standby mode -- a 'hot' standby that is already running takes over quickly (it assumes the active server's IP when heartbeats stop), while a 'cold' standby must start up first, lengthening downtime. Active-active has no takeover step since both servers are already serving.

Load: only active-active spreads load across both servers; in active-passive, only the active server handles traffic.

Shared risk: both patterns add hardware and complexity, and both can lose data if the active system fails before newly written data is replicated to the passive/peer.

Extra requirement for active-active: if the servers are public-facing, DNS must know the public IPs of both servers; if internal-facing, application logic must know about both servers.

Recommendation: for a fast-growing public API, active-active is the better fit because it both removes the takeover delay and spreads the growing load across servers; the team must update DNS with both public IPs and accept the added complexity. (Active-passive with a hot standby would be a reasonable cheaper alternative if load were not a concern.)
common_mistakes: Claiming active-passive loses no data because the passive copy is 'always in sync', overlooking the replication window when the active fails
Forgetting that a cold standby must start up, and quoting near-zero downtime for any active-passive setup
Choosing active-active without accounting for the DNS (or application logic) requirement to know both servers
Treating fail-over as free, ignoring that it adds hardware and additional complexity

exercises.title: Push or Pull CDN: Two Sites, Two Strategies
exercises.problem_statement: You advise two site owners adopting a CDN. Site A is a small marketing site: low traffic, and its content (images, brochures, CSS) changes only a few times a year. Site B is a high-traffic news portal: heavy traffic with content constantly being added and updated. For each site, recommend a push CDN or a pull CDN. Justify each choice by explaining who is responsible for getting content onto the CDN, what happens on the first request, the storage-versus-traffic trade-off, and one staleness or redundancy risk the owner must manage.
hints: Push CDNs receive new content whenever changes occur on your server: you upload directly to the CDN and rewrite URLs to point to it. Pull CDNs grab content from your server when the first user requests it.

Compare the trade-offs: push uploads content only when new or changed (minimizing traffic, maximizing storage); pull minimizes CDN storage but the first request is slower and expired files can be re-pulled before they actually changed.
Match traffic patterns: content placed once and rarely updated suits one model; heavy traffic where only recently-requested content stays cached suits the other.
exercises.expected_solution:
Site A (low traffic, rarely updated) should use a push CDN. The owner takes full responsibility for providing content: uploading directly to the CDN, rewriting URLs to point to the CDN, and configuring when content expires and is updated. Content is uploaded only when it is new or changed, which minimizes traffic but maximizes storage. Sites with small amounts of traffic or content that isn't often updated work well with push: content is placed on the CDN once instead of being re-pulled at regular intervals.

Site B (heavy traffic, frequent updates) should use a pull CDN. Content stays on the origin server and the CDN grabs it when the first user requests it, so the first request is slower until the content is cached; a TTL determines how long content is cached. Pull minimizes storage space on the CDN, and heavy-traffic sites work well because traffic is spread out evenly with only recently-requested content remaining on the CDN. Risk to manage: redundant traffic when files expire and are re-pulled before they actually changed, and generally content can be stale if updated before the TTL expires. Both owners must also accept that CDN costs depend on traffic and that static-content URLs must be changed to point to the CDN.
common_mistakes: Recommending pull for the rarely-updated low-traffic site, causing periodic re-pulls of content that never changed
Forgetting that with a push CDN the owner must upload content and rewrite URLs themselves -- it is not automatic
Ignoring the first-request penalty of pull CDNs when reasoning about user experience
Assuming CDN content is always fresh, overlooking that content updated before the TTL expires will be served stale

exercises.title: Layer 4 vs Layer 7, and Scaling Out Behind the Balancer
exercises.problem_statement: A video platform wants its load balancer to send video-streaming requests to media servers and user-billing requests to security-hardened servers. (a) Explain why a layer 4 load balancer cannot do this and a layer 7 load balancer can, including what information each layer inspects and the performance trade-off. (b) The platform then scales from one app server to ten behind the balancer, and users start getting logged out randomly. Diagnose the cause and give two fixes consistent with horizontal-scaling practice. (c) The team also runs a single internal admin web server and asks whether a reverse proxy is pointless with just one server -- answer with at least three benefits a reverse proxy provides even for a single server.
hints: Layer 4 balancers look at transport-layer info -- source and destination IPs and ports in the header, but not packet contents (they forward packets with NAT). Layer 7 balancers terminate traffic and read the application-layer message: headers, message contents, and cookies.
Random logouts when scaling out usually mean user/session state lives on individual servers. What must servers be for cloning to work, and where can sessions live instead?

Load balancers are useful when you have multiple servers serving the same function; reverse proxies are useful even with one server -- think security, SSL termination, caching, compression, static content.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Routing by request type requires inspecting the application layer: a layer 7 load balancer terminates network traffic, reads the message (header contents, message, cookies), makes a load-balancing decision, then opens a connection to the selected server -- e.g. directing video traffic to video-hosting servers and sensitive billing traffic to security-hardened servers. A layer 4 balancer only sees transport-layer info (source/destination IPs and ports, not packet contents) and forwards packets via NAT, so it cannot distinguish video from billing requests. Trade-off: layer 4 requires less time and computing resources than layer 7, though the impact can be minimal on modern commodity hardware.

(b) The servers are stateful: sessions are stored locally, so a user whose requests land on different instances loses their session. Fixes: make servers stateless (no user-related data like sessions or profile pictures on the server) and store sessions in a centralized data store such as a database (SQL/NoSQL) or persistent cache (Redis, Memcached); alternatively, enable session persistence at the load balancer, which issues cookies and routes a specific client's requests to the same instance. Note that as upstream servers scale out, downstream caches and databases must handle more simultaneous connections.

(c) A reverse proxy is useful even with one server: increased security (hide backend server info, blacklist IPs, limit connections per client), SSL termination (decrypt requests/encrypt responses so the backend doesn't, removing the need for X.509 certificates on each server), caching of responses, compression of responses, and serving static content (HTML/CSS/JS, photos, videos) directly. Caveat: it adds complexity and a single reverse proxy is itself a single point of failure.
common_mistakes: Claiming a layer 4 balancer can route on URLs or cookies -- it only sees transport-layer headers (IPs and ports), not packet contents
Fixing the session problem only with sticky sessions and not recognizing the underlying statefulness that limits horizontal scaling
Asserting a reverse proxy is useless with one server, confusing its role with load balancing across multiple servers
Forgetting that the balancer or proxy itself becomes a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck if under-resourced or misconfigured

exercises.title: Design a Sharding Scheme for a Users Database
exercises.problem_statement: A social application's users database no longer fits on one machine. Design a sharding scheme: (a) propose a sharding function and explain why you rejected sharding by the user's last-name initial; (b) describe the 'power user' hot-spot problem and how your scheme mitigates or at least monitors it; (c) explain what technique reduces the amount of data transferred when shards must be rebalanced; (d) list two costs this scheme imposes on the application (queries/joins) and one thing you must add so that losing a shard does not mean losing data; (e) name two performance benefits sharding brings compared to the single big database.
hints: Common ways to shard a users table are by last-name initial or geographic location -- but think about whether either spreads load evenly, and what a hash-based function gives you.

Data distribution can become lopsided: a set of power users on one shard can increase its load relative to others. Rebalancing adds complexity -- a sharding function based on consistent hashing can reduce the amount of transferred data.
Remember the application-side costs: updated application logic and complex SQL, harder joins across shards, more hardware -- and that you'll want replication on each shard to avoid data loss.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Use a hash-based sharding function over the user ID (consistent hashing). Sharding by last-name initial creates unbalanced distribution because some letters are far more common, concentrating users (and load) on certain shards.

(b) Hot spots: even with even key distribution, a set of power users on one shard can produce increased load on that shard compared to others, making data distribution lopsided. Mitigation: monitor per-shard load and rebalance when skew appears; hashing user IDs at least decouples shard assignment from user attributes that cluster.

(c) Consistent hashing reduces the amount of data transferred during rebalancing, which otherwise adds significant complexity.

(d) Costs: application logic must be updated to work with shards, which can result in complex SQL queries, and joining data from multiple shards is more complex; sharding also adds more hardware and complexity overall. To avoid data loss when a shard goes down, add some form of replication per shard (other shards remain operational, but the failed shard's data needs replicas).

(e) Benefits: less read and write traffic per database, less replication, and more cache hits; reduced index size, which generally improves performance with faster queries; and no single central master serializing writes, allowing parallel writes with increased throughput.
common_mistakes: Choosing an attribute-based shard key (last-name initial, geography) without considering unbalanced distribution and hot shards
Planning rebalancing as a full reshuffle instead of using consistent hashing to limit transferred data
Assuming cross-shard joins work as before, ignoring the added application-logic and SQL complexity
Relying on 'other shards still work' as durability and skipping per-shard replication

exercises.title: Partition an E-Commerce Data Estate
exercises.problem_statement: An e-commerce system stores: (1) order transactions (business-critical, high write volume, growing past single-server limits); (2) a product catalog where name, description, and price are read constantly but stock count and last-ordered date change frequently; (3) log/trace data (low criticality, used occasionally). Design a partitioning scheme that combines the three partitioning strategies: say which strategy you apply to each dataset and why, propose a shard key for orders and justify it against hot partitions, and explain how you arrange partitions so the most critical data is the most available (backup frequency, independent recovery).
hints: Recall the three strategies: horizontal partitioning (sharding) -- same schema, each shard holds a subset such as orders for a set of customers; vertical partitioning -- subsets of fields split by pattern of use; functional partitioning -- data aggregated by bounded context (e.g. invoice data separate from product inventory). They can be combined.

For the shard key: the key must spread workload evenly; using the first letter of a customer's name causes unbalanced distribution because some letters are more common -- a hash of a customer identifier distributes data more evenly. Also pick a key that minimizes future splitting/coalescing of shards.

For availability: identify critical business data (transactions) versus less critical operational data (log files); store critical data in highly available partitions with an appropriate backup plan, back up partitions holding transaction data more frequently, and design partitions so each can be recovered independently.
exercises.expected_solution:
Start with functional partitioning by bounded context: separate order/invoice data, product inventory data, and logging into different data stores. This reduces data access contention between parts of the system and lets each partition use a store matched to its use (e.g. archive older or low-value data in cheaper storage).

Orders: apply horizontal partitioning (sharding) on top -- all shards share the same schema, each holding a subset of orders. Shard key: a hash of the customer identifier, because the key must spread the workload as evenly as possible; a key like the first letter of the customer name causes unbalanced 'hot' partitions since some letters are more common. Also choose the key to minimize future needs to split large shards or coalesce small ones, since those operations are time-consuming and may require taking shards offline (with replicated shards, some replicas may stay online read-only during reconfiguration). Note shards need not be equal in size -- balancing the number of requests matters more -- and no shard should exceed the store's scale limits.

Product catalog: apply vertical partitioning -- put the frequently read, slow-moving fields (name, description, price) in one partition and the dynamic fields (stock count, last-ordered date) in another. Slow-moving data is a good caching candidate, and this reduces I/O and concurrent access.

Availability by criticality: order transactions are critical business information, so place them in highly available partitions with an appropriate backup plan and back them up more frequently than partitions holding logging or trace information; keep data of the same criticality together so it can be backed up together. Design partitions for independent management so a failed partition can be recovered without affecting the others, and remember that replicating critical data across partitions improves availability/performance but introduces consistency issues during synchronization.
common_mistakes: Using only one partitioning strategy when the scenario calls for combining functional, horizontal, and vertical partitioning
Choosing a shard key based on a natural attribute with skewed distribution (e.g. name initial), creating hot partitions
Backing up everything on the same schedule instead of aligning backup frequency with data criticality
Splitting frequently co-accessed fields into separate vertical partitions (e.g. separating stock count from last-ordered date, which are commonly used together)

exercises.title: Pick a Cache Update Pattern per Workload
exercises.problem_statement: Choose a cache update pattern (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead) for each workload and justify the choice with its trade-offs: (W1) read-heavy user-profile lookups where only requested data should occupy cache and brief staleness is acceptable; (W2) account settings where reads immediately after writes must never be stale and users tolerate slower writes; (W3) a burst-heavy event ingestion path where write latency matters most and rare data loss is tolerable; (W4) a dashboard whose hot keys are predictably re-read just after they expire. For W1, also describe the three-trip cost on a cache miss and what mitigates stale data.
hints: Match each workload to the pattern's core behavior: lazy loading on demand; synchronous write to cache and store; asynchronous write to the store; automatic refresh of recently accessed entries before expiration.

Think about the failure/cost profile of each: which pattern risks data loss if the cache dies, which makes writes slow but reads fresh, which delays only the first reader, which backfires if predictions are wrong.

W1 = cache-aside (miss: check cache, load from DB, add to cache, return -- three trips; TTL or pairing with write-through mitigates staleness); W2 = write-through; W3 = write-behind; W4 = refresh-ahead.
exercises.expected_solution:
W1 - Cache-aside (lazy loading): the application looks for the entry in cache, on a miss loads it from the database, adds it to cache, and returns it. Only requested data is cached, avoiding filling the cache with unrequested data -- matching the requirement. Costs: each cache miss results in three trips (noticeable delay), data can become stale if updated in the database (mitigated by setting a TTL that forces an update, or by combining with write-through), and a failed node is replaced by an empty one, increasing latency until it warms.

W2 - Write-through: the application uses the cache as the main data store; the cache synchronously writes each entry to the data store. Writes are slow overall, but users are generally more tolerant of latency when updating data than reading it, and subsequent reads of just-written data are fast with no staleness -- exactly the 'never stale after write' requirement. Downsides: new/replacement nodes miss entries until they are written again (mitigate by pairing with cache-aside), and most written data might never be read (mitigate with TTL).

W3 - Write-behind: add/update the entry in cache and asynchronously write it to the data store, improving write performance for the bursty ingestion path. Trade-offs: possible data loss if the cache goes down before its contents hit the data store (acceptable here), and it is more complex to implement than cache-aside or write-through.

W4 - Refresh-ahead: configure the cache to automatically refresh recently accessed entries prior to expiration. Since the dashboard's hot keys are predictably re-read, this reduces latency versus read-through; the caveat is that inaccurate prediction of which items will be needed yields worse performance than no refresh-ahead at all.
common_mistakes: Choosing write-behind where durability matters, ignoring the data-loss window before cached writes reach the store
Using write-through for write-heavy bursty traffic, making every write pay the synchronous store write
Forgetting that cache-aside data goes stale after database updates unless a TTL (or write-through pairing) is used
Applying refresh-ahead to unpredictable access patterns, where wrong predictions reduce performance

exercises.title: Design an Idempotent Order-Processing Background Job
exercises.problem_statement: Design the background-job architecture for order processing in a web shop: when a user places an order, the UI must stay responsive while a workflow processes the order and the user is later informed of the outcome. Specify: (a) the trigger type (event-driven or schedule-driven) and the concrete mechanism, justifying it against the alternatives; (b) a second, nightly data-retention cleanup task -- which trigger type fits it and what single-instance pitfall must you guard against when the scheduler's host scales out; (c) two result-reporting mechanisms by which the caller can learn the job's outcome, with one suited to an HTTP API caller and one suited to an external system; (d) why the job handler must be idempotent, citing two concrete sources of duplicate execution.
hints: Background jobs are started either by event-driven triggers (a user action or workflow step, e.g. a message placed on a queue that the task listens to) or schedule-driven triggers (a timer). Order placement is a user action; nightly cleanup is periodic.

For result reporting, recall the options: status endpoint the caller polls (Asynchronous Request-Reply), a reply queue with correlation, push notifications through events, a webhook callback URL, or writing status to shared storage.

Queues deliver messages at least once, schedulers can overlap or run duplicate instances when scaled -- what property must the handler have so the same input processed twice produces the same outcome?
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Event-driven trigger: the UI places a message containing the order data on a queue, and the background task listens on that queue and uses the message as input (asynchronous message-based communication). This fits because the job is started by a user action and workflows/order fulfillment are typical event-driven tasks; a schedule would add needless delay between order placement and processing. The UI continues processing interactive requests, minimizing load on the UI and improving responsiveness.

(b) The cleanup task is schedule-driven: a timer invokes it on a recurring schedule -- data-retention cleanup and routine data processing are typical schedule-driven examples. Pitfall: if you scale the compute instance running the scheduler, you create multiple scheduler instances that can start multiple copies of the task; also, if the task runs longer than the scheduler period, another instance may start while the previous one runs. So this task too must be designed idempotent.

(c) For an HTTP API caller: return a status endpoint -- the caller receives a URL/resource identifier when submitting the job and polls it for status (the Asynchronous Request-Reply pattern). For an external system: a webhook -- the caller provides a callback URL at submission and the background task sends an HTTP request to it on completion or error. (Other valid options: a reply queue the caller listens on, using correlation identifiers to match responses to requests; push notifications through published events; or writing status to shared storage the caller monitors.)

(d) Background jobs are especially prone to running more than once for the same logical work item: queues deliver messages at least once, schedulers can overlap if a job outruns the timer interval, and infrastructure restarts can replay partially completed work. Therefore design every handler so the same input produces the same outcome when run multiple times -- e.g. processing the same order message twice must not create two shipments or charge twice.
common_mistakes: Choosing a schedule-driven trigger (polling for new orders) where an event-driven queue trigger gives immediate, decoupled processing
Designing 'fire and forget' with no result-reporting path, leaving the caller unable to learn the job outcome
Assuming exactly-once delivery from the queue and skipping idempotency, causing duplicate side effects like double charging
Ignoring that scaling the scheduler host creates multiple scheduler instances that each start the cleanup task

exercises.title: Spot the Antipatterns in a 'Microservices' Migration
exercises.problem_statement: A team migrated a monolith to twelve services and reports: all services read and write the same shared database schema; every service imports a shared 'common-domain' library of entity classes that must be released in lockstep; clients call each service directly over the internet; each service's configuration values are baked into its container image; and services integrate by emitting generic 'EntityChanged' events containing raw database rows. Releases still require deploying most services together. Identify at least five antipatterns in this design, explain the harm each causes, and propose the corresponding fix.
hints: Start from the definition: microservices are small, independently deployable, loosely coupled services, each responsible for persisting its own data, communicating through well-defined APIs that hide internal implementation.

Check each reported practice against the documented antipatterns: shared data schemas, sharing common libraries between services, exposing services directly to consumers, keeping configuration inside services, generic events, and using database entities as events.
The 'deploy most services together' symptom is the giveaway: which properties (independent deployability, loose coupling) have been lost, and what does each fix restore?
exercises.expected_solution:
1. Shared database schema: causes of coupling include shared database schemas; data storage should be private to the service that owns it, with each service choosing the best storage for its data. Schema changes currently ripple across services. Fix: database-per-service data ownership.

2. Shared common-domain library: sharing common libraries or dependencies between microservices creates tight coupling, making changes risky and widespread, and violates self-containment. Fix: avoid sharing code or data schemas; teams own services end to end and communicate via APIs that model the domain, not internal implementation.

3. Clients calling services directly: exposing microservices directly to consumers results in tight coupling, scalability problems, and security risks. Fix: an API gateway as a clean, manageable, secure entry point that handles cross-cutting concerns (authentication, logging, load balancing) -- while keeping domain knowledge out of the gateway to avoid it becoming a coupling point.

4. Config baked into images: keeping configuration values inside microservices tightly couples them to specific environments and makes deployments harder. Fix: externalize configuration for flexibility and environment portability.

5. Generic events with database rows: using generic events forces consumers to interpret and filter messages, adding complexity; using database entities as events exposes internal service details and fails to convey business intent, leading to tightly coupled, unclear integrations. Fix: specific, atomic, self-contained domain events that convey business intent (and don't depend on past or future events).

The combined symptom -- services that must deploy together -- is the distributed monolith: the system has microservices' complexity (more moving parts, network latency, data-integrity challenges) without the benefits of independent deployment and fault isolation. Underlying remedy: model services on the business domain with DDD-defined bounded contexts, ensure loose coupling and high functional cohesion (functions that change together should be packaged and deployed together), and use messaging frameworks for asynchronous communication.
common_mistakes: Judging the design acceptable because services run in separate containers, missing that independent deployability and data ownership are what define the style
Proposing to fix coupling by adding more shared libraries or a shared 'core' service, which deepens the lockstep problem
Banning all data duplication outright -- avoiding duplication at all costs is itself an antipattern; local copies via materialized views improve autonomy
Putting business rules into the API gateway, making the gateway a dependency that couples services

exercises.title: Classify Subdomains and Draw Bounded Contexts for a Meal-Delivery Startup
exercises.problem_statement: A meal-delivery startup's domain analysis surfaced these business functions: courier dispatch and routing (the company's secret sauce), restaurant menu and order intake, customer accounts, invoicing, a call center, and courier-vehicle maintenance prediction. (a) Classify each function as a core, supporting, or generic subdomain and state what each classification implies for design investment. (b) The 'courier' appears in both dispatch (location, availability) and vehicle maintenance (mileage, repair history, model). Should both areas share one courier model? Apply the bounded-context concept to justify your answer. (c) Dispatch must read customer addresses owned by the accounts context; name two context-map relationship patterns that could govern this integration and when each applies.
hints: Core subdomains provide competitive advantage and deserve detailed modeling and substantial investment; supporting subdomains keep the business operational but don't differentiate; generic subdomains are problems the industry already solved, addressable with existing prebuilt or standard solutions.

Recall the drone example: drone repair and predictive analysis need physical characteristics (maintenance history, mileage, age, model), while scheduling only needs availability and ETA -- a single model for both adds unnecessary complexity and is harder to evolve across teams.

Context-map patterns include Customer-Supplier (upstream provides data/services to downstream, contract negotiated between teams), Open Host Service with Published Language (upstream exposes a well-defined API in a shared format), Anti-corruption Layer (downstream builds a translation layer to protect its model), and Separate Ways.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Core: courier dispatch and routing -- it provides the competitive advantage (the 'secret sauce'), so it requires detailed modeling and substantial team investment. Restaurant menu/order intake is arguably core or supporting depending on differentiation; in this scenario it is central to revenue, so treat it as core (or supporting if undifferentiated). Supporting: invoicing and vehicle-maintenance prediction -- they keep the business operational and need custom development but aren't the source of competitive advantage. Generic: customer accounts and call center -- industry-solved problems best addressed with existing prebuilt or standard solutions rather than custom builds.

(b) No -- define separate bounded contexts. A bounded context is the boundary within a domain where a specific domain model applies, and models need not be consistent across contexts: the maintenance context needs the courier/vehicle's physical characteristics (mileage, repair history, model), while dispatch only needs availability and location. Creating a single model for both introduces unnecessary complexity and makes the model harder to evolve, because changes must satisfy multiple teams. Each model should include only the features and attributes relevant within its context; the same word can mean different things in different contexts (each context has its own ubiquitous language).

(c) Customer-Supplier: accounts (upstream) provides data that dispatch (downstream) depends on, with the contract negotiated between the teams. Open Host Service / Published Language: the accounts context exposes a well-defined API described in a shared format that downstream contexts consume -- especially relevant for microservices, which communicate through well-defined APIs (e.g. OpenAPI descriptions). If accounts were a legacy or convoluted external system, dispatch could add an Anti-corruption Layer -- a translation layer protecting its model from upstream changes.
common_mistakes: Classifying everything customer-visible as core, instead of asking what actually provides competitive advantage
Forcing one canonical 'courier' model across contexts, creating a complex model that multiple teams must coordinate to change
Building custom solutions for generic subdomains like accounts or call center instead of using existing standard solutions
Treating bounded contexts as fully isolated and forgetting to document their interactions in a context map

exercises.title: Design Aggregates for a Hotel-Booking Context
exercises.problem_statement: Within a hotel-booking bounded context you have these concepts: Reservation, Room, Guest, StayPeriod (a start and end date), Price (amount and currency), CancellationRecord (exists only as part of a reservation), and the rule that a reservation's room and guest are managed by other parts of the system with independent life cycles. Design the tactical model: (a) classify each concept as entity, value object, or child entity, justifying by identity and mutability; (b) define the aggregates and their roots, applying the three aggregate-design rules; (c) show how Reservation should refer to Room and Guest; (d) specify how a completed stay should trigger invoicing in another bounded context, distinguishing a domain event from a mere data change.
hints: An entity has a unique identity that persists over time; a value object has no identity, is defined only by its attribute values, and is immutable -- prefer value objects as the default and promote to entity only when you must track identity over time.

Aggregate rules: design small aggregates (only data that must remain consistent within a single transaction); reference other aggregates by identity only; use eventual consistency across aggregates via domain events.

'A record was inserted into a table' is not a domain event; 'a delivery was canceled' is. Aggregates raise domain events after state changes; integration events are published asynchronously through a message broker after the originating transaction commits.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Entities: Reservation, Room, and Guest each have a unique identity that persists over time -- two reservations with identical attributes are still distinct, and a guest remains the same individual even if their name or address changes. Value objects: StayPeriod (a date range) and Price (currency amount) have no identity; they are defined only by their attribute values, are immutable (updates create new instances), and any methods must be side-effect free. CancellationRecord is a child entity of Reservation: it doesn't exist independently (like Confirmation/Notification under Delivery in the drone example).

(b) Aggregates: Reservation, Room, and Guest are separate aggregates, each its own consistency boundary with its own root, because they have independent life cycles managed by different parts of the system. Rules applied: design small aggregates -- include only data that must remain consistent in a single transaction (creating or cancelling a reservation must not lock the room or guest records; combining them forces unrelated updates to compete for the same locks); an aggregate can even be a single entity -- the transactional boundary is what makes it an aggregate. Lookup goes through the root's identifier, and child entities (CancellationRecord) are reached only via the root.

(c) Reference by identity only: Reservation stores a RoomId and a GuestId, not object references -- exactly as Delivery stores DroneId and PackageId. This decoupling maps directly to microservice boundaries.

(d) When a stay completes, the Reservation aggregate raises a domain event such as StayCompleted -- a domain-significant change, unlike 'a row was updated'. Because invoicing lives in another bounded context, publish it as an integration event asynchronously through a message broker after the transaction that originated it commits; the invoicing context consumes it to trigger the invoice (mirroring DeliveryCompleted consumed by the accounts context). This implements eventual consistency across aggregates instead of a single distributed transaction. Also keep behavior inside the entities (e.g. Reservation decides whether it can be cancelled) to avoid an anemic domain model.
common_mistakes: Modeling StayPeriod or Price as entities with IDs instead of immutable value objects compared by attribute values
Building one giant Reservation aggregate that contains Room and Guest, forcing unrelated updates to compete for the same locks
Holding direct object references to other aggregates instead of identifiers (RoomId, GuestId)
