Coordinating cross-aggregate changes with a single transaction rather than raising domain events and accepting eventual consistency

exercises.title: Evaluate a Service-per-Entity Decomposition Proposal
exercises.problem_statement: For the drone-delivery shipping context (aggregates: Delivery, Package, Drone, Account; child entities: Confirmation, Notification, Tag; domain services: Scheduler, Supervisor), an architect proposes one microservice per entity -- seven services including ConfirmationService, NotificationService, and TagService -- arguing 'smaller is always better'. Evaluate this proposal: (a) state the sizing heuristic that bounds a microservice from below and above, and apply it to the seven-service plan; (b) explain which proposed services fail the validation criteria and why; (c) describe what the team should do when in doubt about granularity; (d) give two examples from the drone scenario where nonfunctional requirements justified creating additional services beyond the domain model.
hints: The general principle: design a microservice to be no smaller than an aggregate and no larger than a bounded context. Confirmation, Notification, and Tag are child entities, not aggregates.

Validation criteria include: single responsibility; no chatty calls between services (chattiness suggests functions belong together); small enough for a small team; no interdependencies requiring joint deployment; not tightly coupled; boundaries that avoid data-consistency problems.
Recall the Ingestion service (created for throughput/load leveling) and the Delivery History service (created because long-term historical storage requirements differ from in-flight operations).
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) The heuristic: a microservice should be no smaller than an aggregate and no larger than a bounded context. Aggregates are good microservice candidates because a well-designed aggregate is derived from business requirements, has high functional cohesion, is a boundary of persistence, and is loosely coupled. Confirmation, Notification, and Tag are child entities of Delivery and Package -- below aggregate granularity -- so ConfirmationService, NotificationService, and TagService violate the lower bound. Delivery, Package, Drone, and Account services are legitimate candidates (and the Scheduler and Supervisor domain services -- stateless operations across multiple aggregates -- also make sense as microservices).

(b) The child-entity services fail validation: they don't have independent life cycles, so they would create chatty calls with their parent (a symptom that the functions belong in the same service), tight coupling, interdependencies forcing joint deployment, and data-consistency problems by splitting a consistency boundary (the aggregate) across services.

(c) Be pragmatic -- DDD is iterative. When in doubt, start with more coarse-grained microservices: splitting a service into two later is easier than refactoring functionality across several existing services. Also factor in nonfunctional requirements: team size, data types, technologies, scalability, availability, and security can justify splitting or merging services.

(d) From the scenario: the Ingestion service was added after evaluating throughput needs -- it implements queue-based load leveling by buffering incoming requests that the Scheduler reads. The Delivery History service was split out because the data-storage requirements for historical analysis differ from those for in-flight operations; it listens for DeliveryTracking events and writes them to long-term storage. (Also relevant: Drone and Account belong to other bounded contexts, so the team can either call those contexts directly or create mediating services exposing APIs better suited to the shipping context -- e.g. an anti-corruption layer if the other context is a legacy system.)
common_mistakes: Equating 'micro' with 'one service per entity', ignoring that child entities fall below the aggregate lower bound
Validating only service size and ignoring chattiness, joint-deployment interdependencies, and consistency boundaries
Defaulting to the finest decomposition when in doubt, although coarse-grained first is the recommended pragmatic path
Deriving services purely from the domain model and ignoring nonfunctional requirements like throughput or divergent storage needs

exercises.title: Sync or Async: Wire Up the Delivery Workflow
exercises.problem_statement: You are designing communication for a delivery-scheduling system with these interactions: (I1) clients submit delivery requests that arrive in unpredictable bursts; (I2) a Scheduler orchestrates a user request by calling Account, Package, Drone, and Delivery services and cannot proceed without each one's answer; (I3) when a downstream service fails nontransiently mid-workflow, already-completed steps (e.g. a scheduled drone) must be undone; (I4) delivery status changes must reach a history service today and possibly an analytics service later, without slowing the main workflow. For each interaction choose synchronous API calls or asynchronous messaging and justify the choice; for I3, explain why a distributed ACID transaction is not the answer and what pattern to use instead, including who coordinates it and what property makes retried steps safe.
hints: Synchronous = the caller waits for a response (HTTP/gRPC); asynchronous = the sender doesn't wait. Async advantages include reduced coupling, multiple subscribers via pub/sub, failure isolation, responsiveness, and load leveling -- which of these does each interaction need?

In the drone-delivery design: ingestion used Event Hubs messages for load leveling; the Scheduler called backend services with synchronous REST because it needed a response from each; failures went to a Supervisor via an async message; status changes were published as events with the history service as the first subscriber.

For I3: nontransient failure leaves the transaction partially failed; the remedy is compensating transactions coordinated by a dedicated service (Scheduler Agent Supervisor variation), with operations designed to be idempotent (or checkpointed) so duplicates and resumes are safe.
exercises.expected_solution:
I1 - Asynchronous messaging: bursty ingestion needs load leveling -- a queue acts as a buffer so receivers process at their own rate (in the reference design, the Ingestion service sends asynchronous messages to the Scheduler precisely to implement load leveling).

I2 - Synchronous internal APIs (REST/gRPC): the Scheduler needs a response from each downstream service to carry out the request, and a failure in any downstream service fails the whole operation. The known cost is latency added by calling the backend services in sequence -- with a chain of synchronous dependencies, waiting can add unacceptable latency, so keep the chain short.

I3 - Compensating transactions, not distributed ACID: after a nontransient failure (one unlikely to resolve itself, e.g. invalid input or a crash -- as opposed to a transient fault like a network timeout that retries can resolve), the workflow is in a partially failed state and completed steps must be undone (the scheduled drone must be canceled). The Scheduler puts failed operations onto a dedicated queue (asynchronous message), and a separate Supervisor service reads it and calls cancellation APIs on the services that must compensate -- a variation of the Scheduler Agent Supervisor pattern. Remember compensating measures can themselves fail. To survive Scheduler crashes, either checkpoint each workflow step to a durable store (at a performance cost) or design all operations to be idempotent -- callable multiple times without additional side effects, with downstream services detecting and ignoring duplicate calls.

I4 - Asynchronous pub/sub events: the Delivery service publishes delivery status events (e.g. DeliveryCreated, DeliveryCompleted); any service can subscribe. The history service is the current subscriber, and because the publisher doesn't wait for responses, adding more subscribers (e.g. real-time analytics) doesn't affect the main workflow path. This gives reduced coupling, multiple subscribers, and failure isolation (messages are picked up when a consumer recovers).

Also acknowledge async costs: coupling to the messaging infrastructure, queue latency under load, monetary cost at high throughput, and complexity -- duplicate messages must be handled by de-duplicating or idempotency.
common_mistakes: Using synchronous calls for bursty ingestion, losing the load-leveling buffer and overwhelming downstream services
Trying to span the multi-service workflow with a distributed ACID transaction instead of compensating transactions
Confusing asynchronous I/O (non-blocking thread, an implementation detail) with an asynchronous protocol (sender doesn't wait for a response)
Forgetting duplicate-message handling: without idempotency or de-duplication, retried or redelivered messages corrupt state

exercises.title: Select Encoding Formats for Three Exchanges
exercises.problem_statement: Choose an encoding format for each exchange and justify it: (E1) a public HTTP REST API whose payloads are also placed onto a message queue for asynchronous processing; (E2) a high-throughput internal stream of telemetry records (time-series, all records share a schema) consumed by a stream-analytics system, where producers and consumers must evolve their schemas independently and detect incompatibilities; (E3) a bandwidth-sensitive interservice exchange where both sides are compiled from shared definition files and no one ever reads archived payloads. For E2, explain why JSON is a poor fit and what property of your chosen format supports schema-compatibility checks. State one general rule about proprietary versus well-known formats.
hints: JSON is the standard interchange format for HTTP REST APIs and the most interoperable text format; if you already receive JSON from clients and queue it, re-encoding may not make sense. But avoid JSON for a sequence of records such as time-series data.

Avro serializes with a schema preamble (header applying to a set of records), is recommended for streaming data and tabular/record sets, and its libraries expect the consumer to specify both writer and reader schema before deserializing -- enabling compatibility checks. Stream-analytics platforms natively support JSON, CSV, and Avro.

Protobuf uses strongly typed definition files compiled to language-specific classes; payloads are small, compressed binary -- fast transfer but not human readable, and since the schema is stored externally it's not ideal when you need to read archived data.
exercises.expected_solution:
General rule: use well-known formats instead of a proprietary model -- well-known formats have universally supported community libraries, whereas specialized formats need specific libraries and your business logic may have to work around their API design choices. Also factor in the technology ecosystem (e.g. native format support in your stream-processing service).

E1 - JSON: it is the standard interchange format for HTTP REST APIs and the most interoperable text-based encoding. Since the application receives JSON payloads from clients and places them on a queue, keeping JSON avoids re-encoding; returning cached items directly as JSON can even save deserialize/serialize costs. JSON supports optional fields, aiding forward and backward compatibility, and can be parsed without a schema. Being text-based it isn't efficient over the wire, so minify where possible, and it suits single-record messages or sequences where each message has a different schema.

E2 - Apache Avro: a binary serialization format whose serialized data always includes a schema preamble; because the header applies to a set of records it is well suited to tabular/time-series data, and its smaller encoding size makes it recommended for streaming. Stream-analytics services support it natively. For schema evolution: choose an encoding library that makes compatibility checks between the reader and writer schema -- Avro expects the consumer to specify both writer and reader schema before deserializing, ensuring the consumer is aware of schema versions. JSON is a poor fit here because it's inefficient over the wire and explicitly not recommended for sequences of records such as time-series data.

E3 - Protocol Buffers: strongly typed definition files compiled into language-specific serializer classes (matching the shared-definition setup), producing a small, compressed binary payload for fast transfer on the bandwidth-sensitive link. The downsides are acceptable here: the payload isn't human readable, and the externally stored schema makes it unsuitable for retrieving archived data -- which this exchange never does.
common_mistakes: Choosing JSON for the high-throughput time-series stream, despite the guidance to avoid JSON for sequences of records
Picking Protobuf where archived payloads must be readable later, forgetting the schema lives outside the message
Inventing a custom binary format instead of a well-known one, sacrificing interoperability and community library support
Ignoring schema evolution: choosing a library that doesn't check reader/writer schema compatibility when producers and consumers evolve independently

exercises.title: Pick a Data Store per Service -- and Defend the Rule That Forbids Sharing
exercises.problem_statement: Three services in a delivery platform need storage: (S1) a Delivery service that tracks in-progress deliveries -- users constantly poll the latest status of a specific delivery, reads and writes must be fast, data is short-lived, and no complex queries are run; (S2) a Delivery History service that ingests completed-delivery events for two uses: large-scale analytics over heterogeneous data, and individual lookups by delivery ID after completion; (S3) a Package service storing non-relational package records needing long-term storage, high write throughput, and simple lookups by package ID without joins. Recommend a storage type for each (and explain why S2 needs two stores). Then a teammate proposes letting S2 read S1's tables directly 'to save an API call' -- explain precisely why this is forbidden and what is and isn't allowed about sharing database infrastructure.
hints: Match store to read/write profile: S1 emphasizes throughput over long-term storage (an in-memory cache/key-value store like Redis fits); S3's data is non-relational with simple ID queries (document database).

S2 has two scenarios with different requirements: schema-on-read analytics over large datasets (a data-lake / HDFS-compatible store, partitioned by date) versus ID-based lookups (which date-partitioned folders make inefficient -- hence a second, document store for a recent subset, with older records archived by a batch process).

The rule: two services shouldn't share a data store because shared schemas couple services -- but services can safely share the same physical database server; the problem is sharing the same schema or reading/writing the same set of tables.
exercises.expected_solution:
S1 - An in-memory, high-throughput key-value store (e.g. Redis): the service requires throughput (read and write) over long-term storage, does no complex queries or analysis, and only fetches the latest status for a specific delivery; the data is short-lived, and after a delivery finishes the history service becomes the system of record.

S2 - Two stores, because the two scenarios have different storage requirements. For analytics: a data-lake store (HDFS-compatible) optimized for data analysis over large datasets with a schema-on-read approach to accommodate various sources, storing time-series data in folders partitioned by date. But that layout makes individual ID-based lookups inefficient -- without the timestamp, an ID lookup requires scanning the entire collection. So also store a subset of recent history in a document database for quick ID lookups, and run an occasional batch process to archive older deliveries (reducing cost while keeping data available for historical reporting from the lake).

S3 - A document-oriented database: the package data isn't relational, and the requirements are long-term storage, high write throughput (achievable with sharded collections), and simple queries by package ID without complex joins or referential integrity constraints. Team familiarity with the technology stack is a legitimate selection factor.

Why S2 must not read S1's tables: each service manages its own private data store and other services can't access it directly. Sharing the underlying data schema creates unintentional coupling -- any schema change must then be coordinated across every service relying on that database, defeating independent deployment, and a shared store prevents each team from optimizing storage for its service's data models and read/write patterns. This polyglot persistence (different store types per service) is the intended outcome. What IS allowed: services can safely share the same physical database server -- problems occur only when they share the same schema or read and write the same set of tables. The correct integration is event-driven: S1 publishes delivery status events with a published schema (JSON Schema, Protobuf, or Avro) and S2 subscribes, possibly building a materialized view suited to its queries, accepting eventual consistency with S1 remaining the source of truth for in-flight deliveries.
common_mistakes: Forcing one database technology on all services for operational simplicity, ignoring each service's distinct read/write profile
Using a single store for delivery history, leaving either analytics or ID lookups badly served (ID lookups over date-partitioned data require full scans)
Interpreting 'no shared data store' as 'no shared database server', when the actual rule targets shared schemas and tables
Letting one service query another's tables directly, coupling both to a schema that can no longer change independently

exercises.title: Twelve-Factor Code Review: Config, Backing Services, and Releases
exercises.problem_statement: Review this deployment description against the first five twelve-factor principles: 'Our app keeps the database URL and S3 credentials as constants in the code. Config is grouped into named environments (development, test, production, plus joes-staging). We shell out to the system's ImageMagick for thumbnails. To migrate from local MySQL to a managed database we plan a code change. When production misbehaves, an engineer SSHes in and patches the running code; our releases have no version identifiers, we just overwrite the previous one.' Identify each violation, explain the principle it breaks, and give the compliant practice -- including the litmus test for config and why releases must be immutable with unique IDs.
hints: Config is everything likely to vary between deploys (resource handles, credentials, per-deploy values). The litmus test: could the codebase be made open source at any moment without compromising any credentials? Twelve-factor stores config in environment variables, granular and orthogonal, never grouped into named 'environments'.

Backing services are attached resources: local MySQL and a third-party-managed database should be swappable by changing only the resource handle in config, with no code changes. System tools like ImageMagick must not be relied on implicitly -- vendor them into the app.

Build converts the repo into a build; release combines build + config and is ready for execution; run launches processes against a selected release. The separation is strict: code cannot be changed at runtime because there's no way to propagate it back to the build stage.
exercises.expected_solution:
1. Credentials as constants in code: violates strict separation of config from code -- config varies substantially across deploys, code does not. Litmus test: the codebase could be made open source at any moment without compromising credentials; this one fails. Fix: store config in environment variables -- easy to change between deploys without code changes, hard to accidentally check in, language- and OS-agnostic.

2. Named environment groups ('joes-staging'): batching config into environments doesn't scale -- as deploys multiply, you get a combinatorial explosion of names and brittle deploy management. Fix: env vars as granular controls, each fully orthogonal, independently managed per deploy.

3. Shelling out to system ImageMagick: twelve-factor apps don't rely on the implicit existence of any system tools -- there's no guarantee the tool exists or is version-compatible everywhere the app may run. Fix: vendor the tool into the app, and declare all dependencies completely via a dependency declaration manifest with dependency isolation at runtime.

4. Code change to swap databases: violates backing services as attached resources. The code must make no distinction between local and third-party services -- both are attached resources accessed via a URL or locator/credentials in config. Swapping local MySQL for a managed database should require changing only the resource handle in config; resources can be attached and detached at will (e.g. replacing a misbehaving database with one restored from backup, no code changes).

5. Patching running code, overwriting releases: violates the strict separation of build, release, and run -- changes at runtime can't propagate back to the build stage. Releases must be an append-only ledger: every release gets a unique ID (timestamp or incrementing number) and cannot be mutated once created; any change creates a new release. This enables rollback to a previous release and keeps the run stage simple -- runtime execution can happen automatically (server reboot, crashed process restarted), so problems that prevent the app from running would otherwise break it in the middle of the night, while build-stage errors at least surface in front of the deploying developer.
common_mistakes: Treating internal application config (like framework wiring/route files) as twelve-factor 'config' -- only values that vary between deploys belong in the environment
Replacing constants with uncommitted config files and stopping there -- files can be checked in by mistake, get scattered across formats and locations, and stay framework-specific
Allowing 'small' hotfixes on production servers, breaking build/release/run separation and making state unreproducible
Reusing or mutating a release after creation instead of cutting a new uniquely identified release

exercises.title: Match Deployment Strategies to Three Services
exercises.problem_statement: Assign rolling update, blue-green deployment, or canary release to each case and justify the choice with its risks and costs: (C1) a payment service where any bad release must be reverted instantly by a traffic switch, and the team can tolerate temporarily doubled resource usage; (C2) a recommendation service whose changes are risky in subtle ways the team can only detect by observing real production traffic on a small subset of users first; (C3) a stateless internal API on a resource-constrained cluster, released frequently with backward-compatible changes. For C3, explain the version-mixing hazard during the update and the practice that makes it safe; for C2, explain why this strategy is the most complex to operate and what infrastructure makes fine-grained traffic shifting possible.
hints: Blue-green: deploy the new version alongside the previous one, validate, switch all traffic at once, and switch back if there's a problem -- but you run twice as many pods during the update.

Canary: roll out to a small subset of clients, monitor real behavior, then widen -- it requires routing requests dynamically to different versions, which coarse replica-count tricks only approximate (10 replicas = 10% increments); a service mesh or traffic-split rules give finer control.

Rolling: new instances start receiving requests immediately as previous ones are removed -- the default in Kubernetes deployments -- but during the update a mix of old and new versions receives traffic.
exercises.expected_solution:
C1 - Blue-green: deploy the new version alongside the previous version, validate it, then switch all traffic at once; if problems appear after monitoring, switch traffic back to the previous version, and delete the old one only when confident. This gives the instant traffic-switch revert the payment team requires. Cost: during the update you run twice as many pods (current and next), so if pods use substantial CPU/memory you may need to scale out the cluster temporarily -- acceptable per the scenario. In Kubernetes this doesn't need a separate cluster: create a new deployment with different labels and flip the service's selector to the new pods.

C2 - Canary release: deploy the updated version to a small subset of clients and monitor the behavior of the new service before rolling it out to all clients -- a gradual, controlled rollout that monitors real data and catches problems before they affect all customers, exactly what subtle traffic-dependent risk demands. It is the most complex strategy to manage because you must route requests dynamically to different versions of the service. Plain Kubernetes is coarse-grained -- with a service spanning two replica sets and 10 total replicas you can only shift traffic in 10% increments -- so use service-mesh routing rules (or platform traffic-split features, e.g. 10% to v2 / 90% to v1, shifting weights as confidence grows) for sophisticated control.

C3 - Rolling update: deploy new instances that start receiving requests immediately as previous instances are removed -- the default behavior when you update a deployment's pod spec, with no doubled resource footprint, fitting the constrained cluster and frequent releases; update history allows rollback. Hazard: during the update a mix of previous and new versions runs and any request can be routed to either version. The practice that makes it safe: for breaking API changes, support both versions side by side until all clients of the previous version are updated (API versioning) -- here the team already ships backward-compatible changes, which is why rolling fits.
common_mistakes: Choosing blue-green on a resource-constrained cluster, forgetting it doubles running pods during the update
Treating a canary as 'just fewer replicas', when replica-count splitting only shifts traffic in coarse increments and real canarying needs dynamic routing
Ignoring that rolling updates serve mixed versions simultaneously, breaking clients when the API change isn't backward compatible
Deleting the previous (blue) version immediately after the switch, eliminating the instant-rollback path

exercises.title: Design Retry Policies for an Interactive Call and a Batch Workflow
exercises.problem_statement: Design transient-fault retry policies for two operations calling cloud services over HTTP: (O1) a user-facing request inside an interactive page load; (O2) a step in a long-running nightly batch workflow that is costly to cancel and restart. For each policy specify: which HTTP status codes you retry and which you never retry (with reasoning); the interval strategy and retry count, justified by the operation's context; and how timeouts interact with the retry schedule. Also state: (a) what you do when a response carries a Retry-After header; (b) when you should prefer a service SDK's built-in retry mechanism over your own; (c) why cloud environments make transient faults 'normal' in the first place (give two reasons).
hints: Retry candidates for HTTP services: status 429 (Too Many Requests) and 5xx server errors; most 4xx client errors (400, 401, 403, 404) indicate problems a retry won't resolve. Don't retry operations that can't succeed.

Use exponential back-off with jitter for background operations, and immediate or regular short-interval retries (few attempts) for interactive operations so users aren't kept waiting; total time (timeouts + delays + attempts) must fit the end-to-end latency requirement or SLO.

Cloud reasons: shared resources are subject to throttling that refuses connections at load thresholds; large numbers of commodity hardware units with dynamic load distribution and automatic recycling/replacement of failed units; more network components in the path; varying internet conditions.
exercises.expected_solution:
Retryable codes (both policies): 429 (Too Many Requests) and 5xx server errors are typical retry candidates. Never retry most 4xx errors (400, 401, 403, 404) -- they indicate problems a retry won't resolve, like requests that can't succeed (e.g. updating an item that doesn't exist). Treat 503 carefully: it may indicate the service failed and won't respond to further attempts.

O1 (interactive): the interval should be short and you should attempt only a few retries -- avoid making users wait, since held-open connections can reduce availability for other users. Use at most one immediate retry (transient faults like a packet collision are often brief), then a short regular interval, then fail. Set a timeout on every outbound call before adding retry logic; the timeout plus delays plus attempts must stay within the page's latency budget.

O2 (batch/long-running): where canceling and restarting is costly, you can wait longer between attempts and retry more times. Use exponential back-off (e.g. 2s, 4s, 8s up to a cap) with jitter -- a small random delay on each interval -- to prevent multiple clients from syncing their retries and creating load spikes. The total of connection-failure time (set by the client timeout), inter-retry delays, and max retries determines the overall operation time, which must stay within any SLO; account for the operation timeout when choosing intervals so a new attempt doesn't launch immediately when the timeout resembles the retry interval. Timeouts that are too long accumulate threads and connections during outages; too short, and operations that would succeed fail prematurely.

(a) Retry-After: follow it -- wait at least the specified duration before the next attempt; this server-provided signal reflects the service's recovery timeline and takes precedence over your client-side back-off calculation.

(b) Prefer the built-in SDK retry mechanism when one exists: its policy is typically tailored to the nature and requirements of the target service; deviate only for specific, well-understood requirements.

(c) Transient faults are normal in the cloud because: shared resources are protected by throttling, refusing connections when load reaches thresholds; the platform runs on large numbers of commodity hardware units, delivering performance by dynamically distributing load and reliability by automatically recycling or replacing failed units; more network infrastructure (routers, load balancers) sits between application and services; and network conditions vary, especially across the internet.

Also avoid overly aggressive strategies (too-short intervals, too-frequent retries): they can prevent the target service from recovering, creating a cycle of more requests and further degradation. Use a dead-letter queue so request information isn't lost after all retry attempts are exhausted.
common_mistakes: Retrying 4xx client errors like 400 or 404, which no number of retries will fix
Using the same aggressive retry profile for interactive and background operations, making users wait and holding connections
Omitting jitter so synchronized clients hammer the recovering service in waves
Adding retries without per-call timeouts, letting threads and connections accumulate during outages

exercises.title: Find the Retry Antipatterns in This Incident
exercises.problem_statement: Post-incident review: an API component retries failed calls 3 times; it calls an internal client library that itself retries 3 times; the library's underlying service SDK has its own default retries left enabled. All instances retry at a fixed 2-second interval with no randomization. One worker retries a permanently failing operation in an infinite loop. There are no per-process limits on total retries, and a downstream dependency was kept overloaded for an hour, never recovering. Identify at least five antipatterns in this setup, quantify the multiplication effect of the stacked retries, and prescribe fixes -- including the mechanism that stops calls to an operation that continually fails and the mechanism that caps aggregate retry load.
hints: Stacked layers multiply: one component retrying 3 times calling another that retries 3 times adds up to 9 attempts against the service -- and there's a third layer here. The guidance: avoid duplicated layers of retry code, and turn off or modify built-in mechanisms when implementing retries at a higher level.

Fixed identical intervals across many instances synchronize their retries -- introduce randomization (jitter); avoid regular intervals with high retry counts and prefer exponential back-off with circuit-breaking.

Two safety mechanisms to name: the Circuit Breaker pattern (failures over a threshold within a time window cause immediate errors, with periodic probing to detect recovery) and a retry budget (e.g. no more than 60 retries per minute against a dependency across all requests in the process).
exercises.expected_solution:
Antipatterns and fixes:

1. Cascading/duplicated retry layers: component (3x) * library (3x) already yields 9 attempts per logical call; with the SDK's built-in retries also enabled (say n attempts), it's 9*n -- e.g. 27 with three SDK tries. Fix: avoid duplicated layers of retry code; implement retries at one level and turn off or modify built-in mechanisms below it (this is the Retry Storm antipattern risk).

2. Fixed regular interval, no randomization: multiple instances send retries simultaneously, creating synchronized load spikes. Fix: introduce randomization (jitter) into retry intervals; avoid regular intervals against shared cloud services, preferring exponential back-off combined with circuit-breaking.

3. Endless retry loop: never implement an endless retry mechanism -- it prevents the resource from recovering from overload, prolonging throttling and refused connections. Fix: a finite number of retries, escalating to the Circuit Breaker pattern.

4. No aggregate limit: per-request retry limits alone can't prevent many concurrent requests each retrying a few times from collectively overwhelming a struggling downstream service. Fix: a retry budget limiting total retries across all requests in the process (e.g. at most 60 retries per minute against a dependency); when exhausted, fail immediately instead of retrying. This can make the difference between a localized capacity problem and a cascading failure.

5. No circuit breaker for continually failing operations: a retry strategy caps attempts per operation but doesn't stop the application from starting over on the next request (e.g. each new customer order re-triggers the full retry sequence against a permanently failed service). Fix: Circuit Breaker -- when failures within a time window exceed a threshold, requests return to the caller immediately as errors; the application then periodically tests the service at long intervals (minutes to hours depending on criticality) to detect recovery. Meanwhile, fall back: another service instance in a different datacenter, a simpler compatible service, queueing requests for later, degraded functionality, or an honest unavailability message.

Additional required hygiene: centralize retry-policy values (intervals, counts) in configuration read at runtime rather than hard-coding them in multiple places, so they can be tuned without restarts; log retry attempts (as warnings, not errors), distinguish throttling from connection faults in log entries, measure overall elapsed time, and alert on rising failure rates, average retries, and time-to-success. Test the strategy under fault injection and high load before production. Aggressive retries also harm neighbors on shared services -- and their retries harm you.
common_mistakes: Counting stacked retries additively (3+3) instead of multiplicatively (3*3=9 per layer pair)
Leaving SDK built-in retries enabled underneath custom retry logic, silently multiplying attempts
Adding only per-request retry caps and no process-wide retry budget, so concurrent requests still swamp the dependency
Logging every transient retry as an error, flooding monitoring with false alerts instead of warning-level entries

exercises.title: Design Health and Availability Monitoring for Order Placement
exercises.problem_statement: An e-commerce platform's order-placement feature depends on an order repository and a payment subsystem. Design its health and availability monitoring: (a) specify the traffic-light health model and the alerting latency target for an unhealthy component; (b) list four raw data sources you would wire up to detect 'is it up?' failures, including one that works even when no real users are active; (c) explain how the availability of the order-placement feature is derived from its dependencies and why per-subsystem visibility matters; (d) using the standard formula, compute the availability percentage for a 30-day month (43,200 minutes) in which the repository was down 90 minutes and the payment subsystem separately down 40 minutes (no overlap), and state what definition you must pin down before reporting this number.
hints: Health monitoring should raise an alert within seconds if any part is unhealthy, using red (unhealthy/stopped), yellow (partially healthy/reduced functionality), green (healthy); a comprehensive system shows the status of each subsystem and component.

Raw-data sources include: tracing user request execution (which succeed/fail, duration), synthetic-user monitoring (simulated user actions following predefined steps), logging exceptions/faults/warnings, monitoring endpoints (health endpoints pinged on a schedule), third-party service health, and ambient performance info (CPU, I/O, network).

%Availability = ((Total Time - Total Downtime) / Total Time) * 100. If the feature depends on both subsystems and the outages don't overlap, the feature's downtime is their sum. The definition of 'downtime' itself depends on the service (e.g. a minute counts as unavailable if all continuous HTTP requests during that minute error or get no response).
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Use traffic-light health signals: red = unhealthy (the system stopped), yellow = partially healthy (running with reduced functionality), green = healthy. The system should raise an alert within seconds if any part is unhealthy, and the health-monitoring view should show the status of each subsystem and component so you can determine which parts function normally and which have problems.

(b) Data sources: (1) trace the execution of user requests to determine which succeed or fail and how long each takes; (2) synthetic-user monitoring -- simulate user actions through a predefined series of steps and capture each step's results, which detects failures even with no real traffic; (3) log exceptions, faults, and warnings from trace statements in application code and from event logs of referenced services; (4) expose and monitor health endpoints -- one per functional area -- which the monitoring system pings on a defined schedule, collecting success/fail; plus ambient performance information (background CPU, I/O, network activity) and the health of third-party services. Record all timeouts, network connectivity failures, and connection retry attempts, time-stamping everything.

(c) The availability of the order-placement feature depends on the availability of the repository storing order details and the payment subsystem handling transactions. The monitoring system must capture availability data for these low-level factors and aggregate them into the overall picture, while keeping current and historical per-subsystem views -- so you can correlate failures with specific activities, see which services fail during peak hours, and identify the reasons for unavailability (service not running, lost connectivity, timeouts, error code responses).

(d) Non-overlapping outages on serial dependencies sum: total downtime = 90 + 40 = 130 minutes. %Availability = ((43,200 - 130) / 43,200) * 100 = (43,070 / 43,200) * 100 = 99.70%. Before reporting, pin down the definition of downtime for this service -- definitions vary; for example, one build service counts a minute as downtime only if all continuous HTTP requests during that minute return an error code or no response. This formula and definition are what you would use for SLA monitoring.
common_mistakes: Relying only on real-user traffic for detection, so overnight failures go unnoticed -- synthetic users cover quiet periods
Building a single binary up/down signal with no per-subsystem breakdown, making diagnosis slow
Multiplying component availabilities measured after the fact instead of summing the feature's actual non-overlapping downtime in the formula
Reporting an availability percentage without first defining what counts as 'downtime' for the service

exercises.title: Design a Telemetry Collection and Retention Pipeline
exercises.problem_statement: A global application runs hundreds of compute instances that emit trace logs, event logs, and performance counters. Design the telemetry pipeline: (a) choose pull (monitoring agents) or push collection at the node level and justify it for at least one data type; (b) the central store is being overwhelmed by write bursts and you must not lose audit/billing records -- insert the right architectural component between collectors and storage and explain the delivery guarantee and scaling options it provides; (c) describe the consolidation step that merges per-node views, naming the piece of data that lets records from different nodes be tied to one business operation, and one cleanup it enables; (d) define a storage and retention plan: where alerting data lives versus analysis data, what happens to minute-level performance metrics older than a month, which data is kept indefinitely, and what must be scrubbed before storage.
hints: A monitoring agent is a separate local process that periodically retrieves locally collected telemetry and writes it to shared central storage -- it works well for data naturally pulled from a source (e.g. SQL Dynamic Management Views, queue lengths). For multi-datacenter systems, consolidate region by region before central aggregation.

A message queue between collectors and a storage-writing service provides at-least-once semantics so posted data isn't lost; the queue buffers so the writer drains at its own pace; you can prioritize urgent messages, run multiple writer instances, or use an event hub for very high volumes.

For retention: alerting data needs fast, query-optimized storage; down-sample old data (consolidate minute-by-minute indicators older than a month into an hour-by-hour view); metering/billing data may need to be saved indefinitely and audit/security data archived per regulation; never record passwords or personal information.
exercises.expected_solution:
(a) Use the pull model with local monitoring agents: a separate process on each node periodically retrieves locally captured telemetry (trace logs, event logs, performance counters) and writes it to centralized shared storage. Agents suit data naturally pulled from a source, like SQL Server Dynamic Management Views or a message-queue length. (Push -- components actively sending to a passive receiver -- is the alternative; either works at small scale, but at hundreds of instances the flood of data can overwhelm a single central location's I/O bandwidth.) In a multi-datacenter system, collect and consolidate data region by region first, then aggregate regional data centrally; batch less-urgent transfers to save bandwidth but don't delay time-sensitive data indefinitely.

(b) Insert a message queue: agents post telemetry to the queue, and a separate asynchronous storage-writing service takes data from the queue and writes it to shared storage. The queue provides at-least-once semantics, ensuring queued data isn't lost once posted -- protecting auditing and billing records -- and acts as a buffer so the writer retrieves and writes at its own pace. Scaling/priority options: prioritize messages that must be handled quickly (Priority Queue pattern), use different channels/topics to route data by required analysis type, run multiple storage-writing service instances, and use an event hub to dispatch very high event volumes across compute resources.

(c) A consolidation/cleanup service amalgamates per-node data into the system-wide view: records carrying the same correlation information -- an activity ID -- can be merged, which matters because a user's operation may start on one node and continue on another after failover or load balancing. Consolidation also detects and removes duplicated data (possible because the queue delivers at least once). Emit telemetry in an agnostic, self-describing format (JSON, MessagePack, Protobuf) so processing pipelines can be composed; the collection process must be fail-safe and not trigger cascading errors.

(d) Store data per purpose: alerting data must be accessed quickly, so keep it in fast data storage, indexed/structured for the alerting system's queries -- possibly formatted and saved locally per node so a local alerting instance can notify quickly; less urgent reporting/trend data goes to stores supporting data mining and unplanned queries (e.g. performance counters in a SQL database for ad-hoc analysis, trace logs in a document store, security information in HDFS, full-text-searchable data in Elasticsearch); the same data can go to multiple destinations for different uses (e.g. performance counters also feeding billing). Retention: keep a consolidated online view of performance data for a finite period; down-sample historical data -- consolidate minute-by-minute indicators older than a month into an hour-by-hour view -- to cut storage cost while preserving trends; save metering/billing data indefinitely and archive audit/security data per regulatory requirements, encrypted or otherwise protected; and never record users' passwords or other personal information -- scrub those details before storing.
common_mistakes: Writing telemetry from every node directly to central storage, creating an I/O bottleneck and losing data during bursts
Skipping the queue (or using one without at-least-once semantics) on the path carrying audit and billing records
Omitting correlation/activity IDs, making it impossible to merge a single operation's records across nodes after failover
Retaining raw minute-level metrics forever instead of down-sampling old data, exploding storage costs
